### Task 1 – Get yourself running {#task-1-get-yourself-running}

*Workspace:* open the workspace folder in your IDE, run `source("R/check_setup.R")`, and render the report once. *Browser lab:* wait for the engine to finish downloading, then run the three cells of the setup check and confirm that the panel has 270 rows. The warm-up that follows sorts four scenarios into the three Rs.

### Task 2 – Meet the panel, name the estimand, draw the graph {#task-2-meet-the-panel-name-the-estimand-draw-the-graph}

The task has three parts, taken in order. First, look at the **country-year panel** (`europeanisation_cy.csv`), 270 country-years with unemployment and GDP growth alongside several EU-framing measures, and find the countries that move sharply around 2009, because the fixed-effects models use that variation within countries. Second, write the **estimand statement**: the unit-specific quantity, the target population, the aggregation. Third, complete the **causal graph**: take the `#` off the arrows that you are willing to defend, check which adjustment set the graph then implies, and write two sentences on what two-way fixed effects adjust for and what they cannot fix. The [causal-graphs companion module](../../companion/dags.qmd) works the material through slowly.

### Task 3 – Reproduce a recorded result {#task-3-reproduce-a-recorded-result}

Choose one of the three analysts whose results rest on aggregate data, and refit the analysis until the value on record comes back to the third decimal. The Task 3 table of the [browser lab](../../lab.qmd#task-3-reproduction) gives the data, the model and the value on record for each of the three. *Workspace:* the three reproductions are written out in the working script and in Task 3 of the report. *Browser lab:* each analyst has cells of its own, with gaps to fill, a hint and a full solution.

### Task 4 – Work the menu {#task-4-work-the-menu}

This task is **exploratory**. Try several specifications from the [specification menu](../../menu.qmd) with `try_spec()`, changing one decision at a time, and compare them with `my_experiments()`. Then choose the one that you would defend, and `submit_exploration()` puts it on the live [class chart](../../class-results.qmd) as an **exploratory** result.

### Task 5 – Declare one specification, run it, report it {#task-5-declare-one-specification-run-it-report-it}

Pick ONE specification from the curve, one option for each of the fourteen decisions on the menu, and complete the preregistration block **before you run that specification**. Then translate the declaration into model syntax yourself, since `build_model()` accepts only code that matches what you declared, run it, and let `report_result()` put it on the chart as a **declared** result beside the exploratory ones.

Task 4 and Task 5 run identical code. What separates them is that an exploratory specification can have been chosen because of its result and a declared one cannot, and you submit twice so that the two sets of results can be compared side by side.
